query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Minor boron addition (~1–2 at.%) to the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy will strengthen grain boundaries and reduce cracking while preserving the alloy’s magnetocaloric and barocaloric performance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or arc-melted (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy, free of rare-earth elements, with known large caloric response but prone to mechanical degradation.
generation.intervention: Doping the alloy with a small amount of boron (~1–2 at.%) via vacuum induction melting followed by short annealing to promote intergranular bonding phases or grain-boundary strengthening.
generation.conditions: Up to 2 T magnetic fields and compressive loading up to roughly 300 MPa, in the temperature range where the original alloy shows a sizable caloric effect (300–400 K).
generation.structural_mediator: Boron-stabilized intergranular regions or second-phase precipitates at grain boundaries that mitigate crack nucleation and propagation under stress.
generation.mechanism: Boron addition is hypothesized to reduce grain-boundary brittleness by forming cohesive boundary phases, thereby maintaining intergranular integrity during repeated mechanical or magnetic loading cycles, without interfering with the first-order magnetocaloric transformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped alloy, the boron-doped samples will show higher compressive fracture strength under applied loads while exhibiting a comparable magnetocaloric and barocaloric response near their transition temperature.
generation.baseline: Unmodified (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 samples that exhibit high caloric performance but are mechanically fragile and prone to cracking.
generation.boundary: Applicable within the doping range of ~1–2 at.% B; tested under 0 to ~2 T magnetic field, compressive stresses up to ~300 MPa, and temperatures close to the alloy’s caloric transition region (~300–400 K). The outcome may be sensitive to doping level and heat-treatment schedule.
generation.uncertainty: No direct evidence of boron doping in MnNiSi–FeCoGe is available, so the actual effect magnitude and microstructural pathways remain partly unknown.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of boron-doped (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloys with varying boron content (0–2 at.%), then compare mechanical and caloric properties to the baseline, undoped alloy.
measurements: Compressive strength at room and elevated temperatures under loads up to ~300 MPa
Adiabatic temperature change and entropy change under magnetic fields up to ~2 T
Microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM) of grain boundaries and boron-containing phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped alloys exhibit either (1) no improvement in crack resistance or compressive strength relative to the baseline, or (2) a clear reduction in magnetocaloric or barocaloric performance beyond typical sample-to-sample variability, then the hypothesis is falsified.

chosen.why: Incorporating a small boron addition into the MnNiSi–FeCoGe matrix can improve bonding at grain boundaries and thereby reduce crack formation under stress without significantly degrading the caloric response. Prior studies on doping in similar alloy families hint that modest boron levels promote beneficial intergranular phases or strengthen grain boundaries. A decisive experimental test that would falsify this hypothesis is to measure both the compressive strength and adiabatic temperature change at various doping levels under relevant magnetic and mechanical loads; any substantial deterioration of the caloric effect or mechanical integrity outside of expected improvements would refute the proposed mechanism.
